title: Why Are Some Rooms Hotter Than Others?
h1: Why Are Some Rooms in Your House Hotter Than Others?
description: Some rooms run hotter because of leaky attic ducts, poor return air, sun exposure or thin insulation. Learn how to find the cause and which fixes really work.
quick_answer: Some rooms run hotter than others because they get less cool air, gain more heat, or both. Common causes are leaky or crushed ducts in the attic, rooms at the end of long duct runs, closed doors with no return air, big sunny windows, thin attic insulation and second floors. A dirty filter or an AC that's struggling makes all of these worse.
body:
If the living room feels fine but the back bedroom feels like an oven, you're not alone. Hot rooms are one of the most common comfort complaints we hear, especially in inland neighborhoods during summer. The cause is usually a mix of how much cool air reaches the room and how much heat the room picks up.

Is the room getting enough air?

Hold your hand up to the supply vent in the hot room and compare it to a vent in a comfortable room. If the airflow is noticeably weaker, the room isn't getting its share. Common reasons include:

  • Leaky or disconnected ducts. In most Southern California homes, ducts run through the attic. A loose connection or tear can dump cool air into the attic before it reaches the room.
  • Crushed or kinked flex duct. Storage boxes, foot traffic or sagging can choke a duct down.
  • Long duct runs. Rooms far from the air handler often get less air.
  • Undersized ducts for the size of the room.
  • Closed or blocked vents under furniture or rugs.
  • A dirty filter or coil that cuts airflow for the whole house.

Can the air get out of the room?

Air needs a path back to the system. Many homes have one central return in a hallway. When a bedroom door is closed, the room pressurizes and less cool air can come in. If a room feels better with the door open, return air is likely the issue.

Fixes include transfer grilles, jumper ducts that connect the room to the hallway, or adding a dedicated return.

Is the room picking up extra heat?

Some rooms just gain more heat than others:

  • Rooms with large west- or south-facing windows
  • Rooms over a garage or with vaulted ceilings
  • Second-floor rooms right under the roof
  • Rooms with thin or missing attic insulation above them
  • Bonus rooms and additions that were added onto the original system
  • Rooms with computers, TVs or gaming equipment running all day

Window coverings, solar screens and better attic insulation can make a big difference here. Air sealing the ceiling also helps keep attic heat from leaking down.

How can I narrow down the cause?

Try this simple process:

  1. Replace the air filter and make sure every vent is open.
  2. Put inexpensive thermometers in a few rooms and check them at the same times of day.
  3. Compare airflow at the vents in hot and comfortable rooms.
  4. Test whether the room improves with the door open.
  5. If you can do it safely, look in the attic for loose or crushed ducts.
  6. Note whether the room is only hot in the afternoon, which points to sun exposure.

Write down what you find so a technician can see the pattern quickly.

What fixes work best?

The right fix depends on the cause:

  • Duct sealing and repair for leaks and disconnections
  • Airflow balancing using dampers to send more air to the hot room
  • Return air improvements for rooms that get better with the door open
  • Attic insulation and air sealing for rooms that heat up from above
  • Zoning for two-story homes or houses with very different areas
  • A ductless mini-split for a bonus room, addition or garage conversion the main system can't handle

If the whole house struggles on hot days, the AC itself may need service. Low refrigerant, a dirty outdoor coil or a weak part can cut cooling capacity. Leave refrigerant and electrical work to a technician.

It often takes more than one fix. A hot upstairs bedroom, for example, might need a sealed duct, a return path and better attic insulation before it feels like the rest of the house. Tackling the biggest cause first usually gives you the most noticeable change, and you can decide on the rest from there.

Our air conditioning technicians can test airflow room by room, check the system and recommend the fix that matches the cause. For duct leaks, our air duct team handles sealing and repair.
faqs: Why is one bedroom always hotter than the rest of the house?

Usually it's either getting less cool air, from a leaky, crushed or long duct, or gaining extra heat from sun, a garage below or thin attic insulation. Closed doors without a return path also play a part.
Will a bigger AC fix a hot room?
Usually not. If the room isn't getting enough air or is gaining extra heat, a bigger system just cools the rest of the house faster. Fixing ducts, return air or insulation works better.
Does closing vents in other rooms push more air to the hot room?
Only a little, and closing too many vents can hurt the system by raising duct pressure. Adjusting dampers on the branch ducts is a better way to shift air.
Is a mini-split a good fix for a hot room?
For a room the main system can't reach well, like a bonus room or converted garage, a ductless mini-split is often the most effective fix. It gives that room its own cooling and heating.
